name: Southwest Route
approach: Four Brothers sits on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and the standard approach starts at the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, ~2,375 ft), reached via SR 903 north from Cle Elum ~17 mi, then Cooper Lake Rd/FR-46 roughly 9-10 mi to the signed trailhead. From the trailhead the trail drops briefly to a crossing of the Kachess River, then climbs to a junction with the Little Kachess Trail (#1312) at about 0.25 mi. Around 1.3 mi it passes an old mine site and shortly after crosses Mineral Creek itself, entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary. The next stretch runs high above the creek through old-growth forest and several brushy former avalanche paths - expect deadfall and slow going here, especially early season. Near the 4-mile mark the trail crosses a side creek (the last dependable water before the basin) and then climbs steeply, gaining roughly 1,500 ft in the final mile-plus to Upper Park Lake (~4,900 ft, about 5.4 mi from the trailhead). From the Park Lakes basin, leave the trail and go cross-country up mixed heather benches and slabby rock toward the saddle on Chikamin Ridge, staying to the north side of the Four Brothers - the four cliffy summit points are unmistakable and form steep, technical terrain that should be flanked rather than climbed directly from below. Once on the ridge crest, traverse back to the base of the southwest-facing gully/slope system that gives this route its name, roughly 6.5-7 mi and about 4,000 ft of gain from the car. Expect lingering snow in the gully well into July, loose stacked talus higher up, and real routefinding complexity picking a line through the pinnacle/cliff-band maze - this is the part of the outing that most often proves the crux, more so than any single move.

waypoints.name: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331)
waypoints.note: Signed trailhead at the bottom of the Cooper Pass valley off FR 4600; ford the Kachess River (logs or wade) just past the sign, and self-issue a wilderness permit and display a Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 80, go north on Bullfrog Road to SR 903 and follow it through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake to Cooper Lake Road (FR 46), about 17 miles. Turn left on FR 46, pass the Cooper Lake turnoff and continue about 7 miles to Cooper Pass, then stay on the main road about 3 miles down to the signed Mineral Creek trailhead in the valley. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, plus a free self-issued wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Little Kachess Trail #1312 junction
waypoints.note: Stay right/north on Mineral Creek Trail #1331; the left fork drops to Little Kachess Lake.
waypoints.directions: From the sign the trail drops straight to the Kachess River, which is crossed on logs or waded — there is no bridge. Climb briefly on the far side to the first fork and stay right and north on #1331; the left branch drops away toward Little Kachess Lake.

waypoints.name: Old mine and mineshaft
waypoints.note: Trail passes an abandoned mining mill with a nearby open mineshaft — a common turnaround for kids, but stay well clear of the shaft opening.
waypoints.directions: Continue north on #1331, which follows an old roadbed before narrowing into real trail and climbing gently through forest above Mineral Creek for a bit over a mile to the old mill site.

waypoints.name: Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary / Mineral Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Mineral Creek entering the wilderness; trail becomes brushy through old avalanche paths from here.
waypoints.directions: A short distance above the mine the trail crosses Mineral Creek itself at the wilderness boundary. It is usually a rock-hop, but it runs high and pushy in early summer.

waypoints.name: Upper creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford a tributary creek; trail angles steeply uphill immediately above this point.
waypoints.directions: Above the boundary the trail traverses well above the creek through old-growth and a string of old avalanche paths, where brush and deadfall make for slow going — budget extra time here, especially early in the season. Ford the tributary creek where the trail meets it; this is the last dependable water before the lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Park Lakes Basin (Upper Park Lake)
waypoints.note: Established camp basin between the two Park Lakes; no campfires allowed, treat/filter water from the lake.
waypoints.directions: Grind up the steep pitch that starts immediately above the ford — roughly 1,500 ft of gain in a bit over a mile, and the sustained crux of the approach — to reach the benches holding the Park Lakes.

waypoints.name: PCT junction near pack camp
waypoints.note: Mineral Creek Trail meets the PCT at a pack camp; leave the trail here and climb heather/slab slopes toward the saddle southwest of the upper lake to gain Chikamin Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Stay on #1331 as it climbs north out of the lakes basin to the pack camp where the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Water at the lakes is the last convenient supply, since the maintained trail ends here.

waypoints.name: Four Brothers (south peak)
waypoints.note: South peak is Class 2 to the summit block with Class 3-4 finish options; several distinct summit points lie along the ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pack camp and climb cross-country up mixed heather benches and rock slabs to gain the crest of Chikamin Ridge. Keep to the north side of the Four Brothers on the way up — the four cliffy points are steep, technical ground meant to be flanked, not climbed directly from below. Once on the crest, traverse back to the southwest-facing slope and gully system that gives the route its name and follow it to the south summit. Picking a line through the pinnacles and cliff bands is the real difficulty, more than any single move; snow lingers in the gully well into July and the talus higher up is loosely stacked, so leave enough daylight to find the correct gully on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Park Lakes basin to the Chikamin Ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: Mineral Creek Trail from the signed trailhead: the Kachess River on logs or a wade, past the old mill site, across Mineral Creek at the wilderness boundary, then a long traverse high above the creek through old-growth and a string of grown-in avalanche paths where brush and deadfall make for slow going. Ford the tributary creek near four miles — the last dependable water before the basin — and grind the steep pitch above it into the Park Lakes benches. Stay on the trail to the pack camp where it meets the Pacific Crest Trail, then leave it and climb heather benches and rock slabs cross-country.
hazards: Loosely stacked talus high on the route
Snow lingering in the gully well into July
Route-finding among four separate rock points that all look like summits from below
Steep heather and dirt near the ridge crest
Cliff bands and pinnacles that have to be threaded rather than climbed
approach_variants.baseFinding: Four Brothers is a cluster of four cliffy points strung along Chikamin Ridge, so the identification problem is which side of the group you are standing on rather than which summit you can see. Gain the crest at the saddle northwest of the group — the col between Chikamin Peak and the Four Brothers — and keep to the north side of the points on the way up. Do not try to climb directly from below on the crest side: that aspect throws up genuinely technical obstacles, and parties bound for Chikamin deliberately detour around it on steep grassy slopes and gully systems. From the col, traverse back southeast onto the southwest-facing aspect. The base of the climb is where the heather benches end and a gully-and-slope system of stacked talus begins beneath the points; that gully is the line, and picking a way through the pinnacles and cliff bands above it is the real crux of the peak, harder than any single move on it. The south peak is the objective. Leave enough daylight to find the same gully going down — improvising a line off the pinnacles late in the day is how parties end up on much steeper ground than they intended.

descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line: down the southwest gully/heather slopes back to the Chikamin Ridge saddle, then back through the gap north of the Four Brothers' cliff bands into the Park Lakes basin and out the Mineral Creek Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - no fixed rappel stations are documented on the Southwest Route itself, and parties who stay on the described line generally do not need to rope up for the descent. Treat any exposed Class 3 downclimbing sections with care, particularly on wet or lichen-covered rock, and a short handline (30-60 ft) is a reasonable option for a party uncomfortable downclimbing the crux step. Note that the adjacent, better-documented Chikamin Peak has a known single-rope bail rappel off its summit horn used by parties who prefer not to downclimb its Class 3 chimney; that anchor is on Chikamin's line, not this route, but if you drift onto that terrain by mistake it's a known escape option. Because Four Brothers' summit block is a genuine cluster of cliffy pinnacles, poor visibility or late-day descent meaningfully raises the chance of wandering onto steeper terrain than intended - budget enough daylight to descend the correct gully rather than improvising a line off the pinnacles.
